# Logging: How a Program Keeps a Diary

> **AI assistant load scope (Claude Code, Gemini):**
>
> **Load when:** using, explaining, or changing the Java `log` package or its Python and TypeScript twins.
>
> **Do NOT load for:** other packages that only call `LogFactory.getLogger`.
>
> **Authoritative scope:** a beginner-level explanation and a short developer reference. The code and
> its Javadoc are authoritative.

This chapter explains the Java package `org.cassandragargoyle.api.log`. Every CassandraGargoyle Java
module uses it to write messages about what the program is doing. You need basic Java: classes, methods, `try`/`catch`,
and arrays.

**What you will learn:**

1. Why real programs write a log, and why `System.out.println` is not enough
2. What a log message is made of: time, level, logger name, and message
3. How log levels work, and how loggers form a tree
4. How the code sends one message to the screen and, in the background, to a file
5. Six traps that surprise almost every beginner

![A small comic: at 3 a.m. the programmer without logging panics, the programmer with logging reads "not a number: x" in the log and knows it is line 25](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

---

## 1. The problem: the program fails, and you were not there

Your program runs on the computer of a user, on a server, or at night. One day the user says: *"It does
not work."* Nothing more. What happened? When? With what data?

The first idea of every beginner is `System.out.println`. It helps for a minute, but it has problems:

| Problem with `println` | What a log does |
| ---------------------- | --------------- |
| You must delete the lines later, or the output is full of noise | You switch messages off with one setting, the code stays |
| You do not know **when** it happened | Every message has a date and time |
| You do not know **which class** wrote it | Every message has the name of its logger |
| Everything has the same importance | Every message has a **level**: error, warning, info, detail |
| The text is lost when the window closes | The messages are also saved in a file |

A **log** is a diary of the program. When something goes wrong, you read the diary instead of guessing.

## 2. One log message, piece by piece

This is a real line that the project writes (you will run the program that wrote it in section 9):

![A log line split into four parts: date and time, the level WARNING, the logger name in square brackets, and the message](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- **Date and time** to the millisecond: *when* it happened
- **Level**: *how serious* it is
- **Logger name**: *who* wrote it; it is usually the full name of the class
- **Message**: *what* happened

## 3. Levels: how serious is it?

Java has seven standard levels. Each level has a number, and a higher number means a more serious
message. You choose a **threshold**: all messages at the threshold and above are shown, everything below
is hidden.

![Table of the seven levels from SEVERE 1000 down to FINEST 300, with the aliases of setLogLevel; with the threshold INFO, SEVERE, WARNING and INFO are shown, the rest is hidden](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The project uses the levels like this (from the Javadoc of [`LogFactory`](LogFactory.java)):

| Level | Use it for | Translated for the user? |
| ----- | ---------- | ------------------------ |
| `SEVERE` | an error; the application shows it in a dialog | yes |
| `WARNING` | a bad or suspicious state; shown in the status bar | yes |
| `INFO` | an important step succeeded; shown in the status bar | yes |
| `CONFIG` | current configuration values | no |
| `FINE`, `FINER`, `FINEST` | details for developers; only in log files | no |

**Try it yourself:** your program reads a configuration file and the file is missing, so the program
uses default values. Which level do you choose? (A good answer is `WARNING`: the program works, but
something is not as expected.)

## 4. Loggers form a tree

Logger names are like package names, with dots. Java puts the loggers into a **tree**: the logger
`org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo.GradeAverage` is a child of `org.cassandragargoyle.api`, and every
logger is a descendant of the **root logger**, whose name is the empty string `""`.

A logger without its own level uses the level of its parent. A message that passes the level check goes
up the tree to the handlers of the root logger. A **handler** is the object that writes the message
somewhere: to the screen or to a file.

![Logger tree: the root logger holds the handlers; org.cassandragargoyle.api gets the level from Logging; GradeAverage inherits it, a class outside the package inherits INFO from the root](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

This is why the package sets the level on `org.cassandragargoyle.api`, and puts the handlers on the root
logger. Section 6 shows a trap that follows from this picture.

## 5. From the idea to the code

The package has three files:

| Type | Kind | What it does |
| ---- | ---- | ------------ |
| [`LogFactory`](LogFactory.java) | class with `static` methods | Creates a logger for a class, and has helpers and annotations |
| [`Logging`](Logging.java) | class with `static` methods | Sets up the handlers, the levels, the format, and the log file |
| [`LogSkipException`](LogSkipException.java) | marker interface | Marks an exception type that the log file should skip |

### Step 1: get a logger

Every class that logs creates its logger once, in a `static final` field. The project code style calls
the field `LOG`:

```java
private static final Logger LOG = LogFactory.getLogger(GradeAverage.class);
```

This is the code of `getLogger`:

```java
public static Logger getLogger(Class clazz)
{
	String className = clazz.getName();
	String resourceBundleName = clazz.getPackage().getName() + ".Bundle";
	try
	{
		return Logger.getLogger(className, resourceBundleName);
	}
	catch (MissingResourceException ex)
	{
		return Logger.getLogger(className);
	}
}
```

- The logger name is the full class name, for example `org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo.GradeAverage`.
- A **resource bundle** is a file `Bundle.properties` with texts in several languages. The logger can use
  it to translate messages for the user.
- When the package has no `Bundle.properties`, Java throws `MissingResourceException`. The code catches it
  and creates a logger without translations. This is the **fallback** pattern: try the better option, and
  use a simpler one when it is not available.

### Step 2: set up logging when the program starts

```java
Logging.initialize("FINE", true, true);
```

The three arguments are the level, "log to the console", and "log to a file". The method does this:

```java
Logger logger = Logger.getLogger(""); // NOI18N

Handler[] oldHandlers = logger.getHandlers();
for (Handler oldHandler : oldHandlers)
{
	logger.removeHandler(oldHandler);
}
if (logOnConsole)
{
	consoleHandler = new CustomConsoleHandler();
	logger.addHandler(consoleHandler);
}
if (logToFile)
{
	logger.addHandler(getFileHandler());
}
setLevel(Level.parse(logLevel));
```

1. It takes the **root** logger (the empty name).
2. It removes all old handlers, so no message is written twice.
3. It adds a console handler and a file handler.
4. It turns the text `"FINE"` into a `Level` with `Level.parse` and sets it on `org.cassandragargoyle.api`.

### Step 3: write a message

```java
LOG.log(Level.FINE, "Reading value {0}", value);
LOG.log(Level.INFO, "Average of {0} grades is {1}", LogFactory.args(count, (double) sum / count));
```

`{0}` and `{1}` are **placeholders**. Java puts the parameters into them only when the message is really
written. With more than one parameter, Java expects an `Object[]` array. The helper `args` makes it
short:

```java
public static Object[] args(Object... args)
{
	return args;
}
```

`Object...` is a **varargs** parameter: Java collects all arguments into an array for you. The method
only returns that array. It is a tiny trick, but it makes every log call easier to read.

### Step 4: where the message goes

![A log call goes through the logger level check to the console handler, which writes at once, and to the file handler, which filters the record, puts it into a queue of up to 1000 records, and lets the background thread Logging Flush write it to the file](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The console handler writes at once. The file handler is different: writing to a disk is slow, and the
program should not wait for it. So the file handler (`NonCloseHandler`) only puts the message into a
**queue** and returns:

```java
private final BlockingQueue<LogRecord> queue = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(1000);
```

```java
if (!queue.offer(record))
{
	// the queue is full: schedule a flush now and wait for a free place
}
...
schedule(delay);
```

A background thread called `Logging Flush` later takes all messages from the queue and writes them:

```java
public void run()
{
	while (true)
	{
		LogRecord r = queue.poll();
		if (r == null)
		{
			break;
		}
		delegate.publish(r);
	}
	delegate.flush();
}
```

This is the **producer-consumer** pattern: one thread produces work and puts it into a queue, another
thread consumes it. You will meet it in games, web servers, and printers.

### Step 5: the log file

`getFileHandler` prepares the file:

```java
File dir = new File(new File(home, "var"), "log");
dir.mkdirs();
cleanUpOldFiles(dir, 10, true);
long pid = ProcessHandle.current().pid();
String fileName = String.format("messages.%06d.log", pid);
```

- The folder is `~/.myapp/var/log/` (`~` is your home folder; see `Places.getUserDirectory()`).
- Files older than **10 days** are deleted when the program starts, so the folder does not grow forever.
- The **PID** (process ID) is the number that the operating system gives to every running program. Each
  run gets its own file. `%06d` writes the number with at least 6 digits and leading zeros, so PID 4242
  becomes `messages.004242.log`.
- When a file with the same name exists, it is renamed to `.1`, and an old `.1` to `.2`.

### Step 6: the format of the line

`CustomFormatter` builds every line with a `StringBuilder`:

```java
sb.append(DATE_FORMAT.format(new Date(record.getMillis())));
sb.append(" ");
sb.append(record.getLevel().getName());
addLoggerName(sb, record);
if (message != null)
{
	sb.append(": ");
	sb.append(message);
}
```

Compare it with the picture in section 2:

| In the picture | In the code |
| -------------- | ----------- |
| date and time | `DATE_FORMAT`, the pattern `dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm:ss.SSS` |
| level | `record.getLevel().getName()` |
| `[logger name]` | `addLoggerName`, which adds `" ["`, the name, and `"]"` |
| message | `formatMessage(record)`, which fills `{0}`, `{1}` |

When the message has an exception, the formatter adds its **stack trace**: the list of methods that were
running when the exception was thrown. In the log file, the line where your code **caught** the exception
starts with `[catch] at` instead of `at`. It helps you find your own code in a long stack trace.

## 6. Traps

Every trap below was tested with the real code.

> **Watch out 1: `initialize` does not know `DEBUG`.** `Logging.initialize("DEBUG", ...)` throws
> `IllegalArgumentException: Bad level "DEBUG"`, because `Level.parse` knows only the Java names (`FINE`,
> `INFO`, ...). The short names `DEBUG`, `D`, `3` work only in `Logging.setLogLevel`.
>
> **Watch out 2: a class outside `org.cassandragargoyle.api` does not get the level.** Look at the tree in
> section 4 again. `initialize("FINE", ...)` sets the level on `org.cassandragargoyle.api` only. A class
> in another package, for example `com.example.MyApp`, inherits `INFO` from the root logger, so its
> `FINE` messages are not shown.
>
> **Watch out 3: an apostrophe in a message with placeholders.** `LOG.log(Level.INFO, "Can't read {0}",
> name)` prints `Cant read {0}`: the apostrophe starts a quoted part, so `{0}` is not replaced. Write two
> apostrophes: `"Can''t read {0}"` prints `Can't read file.txt`. A message without parameters is not
> changed.
>
> **Watch out 4: numbers depend on the language of the computer.** The placeholders format numbers like
> `java.text.MessageFormat`: `2.0` is printed as `2`, and `1234567.5` as `1,234,567.5` in English or
> `1 234 567,5` in Czech.
>
> **Watch out 5: do not build the message with `+`.** `"Reading " + value` builds the text even when the
> level is switched off. `"Reading {0}", value` builds it only when the message is written. For a very
> expensive message, ask first: `if (LOG.isLoggable(Level.FINE)) { ... }`.
>
> **Watch out 6: `LogSkipException` hides the exception only in the file.** The filter
> `DefaultLoggerFilter` is set on the file handler, not on the console handler. A record with such an
> exception is not in the log file, but you still see it on the console.

## 7. How fast is it?

| Part | Cost for your code | Why |
| ---- | ------------------ | --- |
| A message below the level | almost nothing | the logger compares two numbers and stops |
| Console | the time of printing one line | the console handler writes at once |
| File | the time of putting a record into a queue | the background thread writes about one second after the last message (`delay` is 1000 ms) |

Putting a record into the queue takes the same time for a short or a full queue: **O(1)**. Only when the
queue holds 1000 records and is full, your code waits until the background thread makes room.

## 8. The same idea in other languages

The project has logging modules in other languages too:

- Python: [`logging_config.py`](../../../../../../../../python/src/cassandragargoyle/api/log/logging_config.py)
  writes the same line layout as the Java `CustomFormatter` and accepts the same level aliases, mapped to
  the closest Python level (for example `TRACE` becomes `DEBUG`). Its root logger is called `cassandragargoyle`.
- TypeScript: [`typescript/src/log/`](../../../../../../../../typescript/src/log/)

## 9. Use it: an average of grades

This program computes the average of grades. One value is not a number, so it logs a warning and skips it.

```java
package org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo;

import java.util.logging.Level;
import java.util.logging.Logger;
import org.cassandragargoyle.api.log.LogFactory;
import org.cassandragargoyle.api.log.Logging;

public class GradeAverage
{
	private static final Logger LOG = LogFactory.getLogger(GradeAverage.class);

	public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception
	{
		Logging.initialize("FINE", true, true);

		String[] input = {"1", "2", "x", "3"};
		int sum = 0;
		int count = 0;

		for (String value : input)
		{
			LOG.log(Level.FINE, "Reading value {0}", value);
			try
			{
				sum += Integer.parseInt(value);
				count++;
			}
			catch (NumberFormatException ex)
			{
				LOG.log(Level.WARNING, "Skipping a value that is not a number: " + value, ex);
			}
		}

		LOG.log(Level.INFO, "Average of {0} grades is {1}", LogFactory.args(count, (double) sum / count));
	}
}
```

To run it in your copy of the project, save it as
`java/src/main/java/org/cassandragargoyle/api/demo/GradeAverage.java` and run in the `java` folder:

```bash
mvn -q compile dependency:build-classpath -Dmdep.outputFile=cp.txt
java -cp "target/classes:$(cat cp.txt)" org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo.GradeAverage
```

(On Windows, use `;` instead of `:` in the class path.)

Console output:

```text
16/10/2026 13:29:59.779 FINE [org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo.GradeAverage]: Reading value 1
16/10/2026 13:29:59.780 FINE [org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo.GradeAverage]: Reading value 2
16/10/2026 13:29:59.780 FINE [org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo.GradeAverage]: Reading value x
16/10/2026 13:29:59.780 WARNING [org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo.GradeAverage]: Skipping a value that is not a number: x
java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "x"
	at java.base/java.lang.NumberFormatException.forInputString(NumberFormatException.java:67)
	at java.base/java.lang.Integer.parseInt(Integer.java:662)
	at java.base/java.lang.Integer.parseInt(Integer.java:778)
	at org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo.GradeAverage.main(GradeAverage.java:25)
16/10/2026 13:29:59.780 FINE [org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo.GradeAverage]: Reading value 3
16/10/2026 13:29:59.780 INFO [org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo.GradeAverage]: Average of 3 grades is 2
```

The file `~/.myapp/var/log/messages.<PID>.log` has the same lines, with one difference: the line of your
code in the stack trace is marked.

```text
[catch] at org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo.GradeAverage.main(GradeAverage.java:25)
```

The console does not show the mark, because the console handler formats the message before the file
handler finds the line where the exception was caught.

> **Note:** the warning uses `+` on purpose, so that you can compare it with Watch out 5 and improve it
> in exercise 6.

## 10. Exercises

Try each exercise on your own first, then check your answer in section 13.

**1.** You change the first line of `main` to `Logging.initialize("WARNING", true, true)`. Which lines
of the console output are left?

**2.** The average of 1, 2, and 3 is `2.0`. Why does the log say `is 2`?

**3.** What does `LOG.log(Level.INFO, "Don't stop {0}", "me")` print? How do you fix it?

**4.** Which level does `Logging.setLogLevel("d")` set?

**5.** Your program runs with PID 4242. What is the name of its log file?

**6.** Change the warning in `GradeAverage` to use a placeholder instead of `+`, and add an `INFO`
message at the end with the number of skipped values.

**7.** *(Challenge.)* Create an exception class `HarmlessException extends RuntimeException implements
LogSkipException`, log it with `LOG.log(Level.WARNING, "harmless", new HarmlessException("boom"))`, and
compare the console with the log file. Explain the difference with the picture in section 5, step 4.

## 11. Words to remember

| Term | Meaning |
| ---- | ------- |
| Log | a diary of the program: messages with time, level, and source |
| Level | how serious a message is; a threshold hides the less serious ones |
| Logger | the object that your class uses to write messages; it has a name |
| Root logger | the top of the logger tree, its name is `""` |
| Handler | the object that writes messages somewhere (console, file) |
| Formatter | the object that turns a message into a line of text |
| Placeholder | `{0}`, `{1}` in a message; replaced by parameters |
| Varargs | `Object...`: a parameter that takes any number of arguments as an array |
| Queue | a list where the first item in is the first item out |
| Producer-consumer | one thread puts work into a queue, another thread takes it out |
| PID | the number of a running program, given by the operating system |
| Stack trace | the list of methods that were running when an exception was thrown |

## 12. Reference for developers

### Public surface

| Member | Purpose |
| ------ | ------- |
| `LogFactory.getLogger(Class)` | Logger named after the class, bound to `<package>.Bundle` when it exists |
| `LogFactory.args(Object...)` | Returns its arguments as an array, for log calls with several parameters |
| `LogFactory.logDebugWithTrace(String, boolean)` | Logs at `FINE` with the current call stack when the condition is true and the system property `cassandragargoyle.debug` is `true` |
| `LogFactory.LOG_IGNOREDLOGGERS`, `LOG_FORCEDMESSAGES`, `LOG_SHOWNMESSAGES` | NetBeans layer paths `CassandraGargoyle/Log/IngoredLoggers/`, `.../ForcedMessages/`, `.../ShownMessages/` |
| `LogFactory.IgnoreLoggerForUI` | Annotation on a logger field (`@Target FIELD`) |
| `LogFactory.ForcedLogMessages`, `LogFactory.ShownLogMessages` | Annotations with message ids (`@Target TYPE, METHOD, CONSTRUCTOR`) |
| `Logging.initialize(String, boolean, boolean)` | Replaces the root handlers with a console and a file handler; the level must be a JUL name |
| `Logging.setLogLevel(String)` | Resolves the aliases below and calls `initialize(level, true, true)`; logs a warning for an unknown level |
| `Logging.setLevel(Level)`, `Logging.getLevel()` | Level of `org.cassandragargoyle.api`, `org.apache.cxf.wsdl.service.factory`, `com.sun.xml`, and of the console handler |
| `Logging.FORMATTER`, `Logging.FILTER`, `Logging.DATE_FORMAT` | The project formatter, the default filter, and the date pattern |
| `LogSkipException` | Marker interface: the default filter drops records whose thrown value implements it |

The three annotations have `RetentionPolicy.SOURCE`. The NetBeans `layer.xml` annotation processor reads
them; they are not in the class files.

### Level aliases of `setLogLevel`

| Alias (case-insensitive) | Level |
| ------------------------ | ----- |
| `TRACE`, `T`, `4` | `ALL` |
| `DEBUG`, `D`, `3` | `FINE` |
| `INFO`, `I`, `2` | `INFO` |
| `WARNING`, `W`, `1` | `WARNING` |
| `ERROR`, `E`, `0` | `SEVERE` |

Other values are passed to `Level.parse` unchanged.

### Handlers

- **Console**: `CustomConsoleHandler`, UTF-8, `Logging.FORMATTER`, level from `setLevel`, no filter.
- **File**: `~/.myapp/var/log/messages.%06d.log` (PID), level `ALL`, `Logging.FILTER`, asynchronous
  through `NonCloseHandler` (queue of 1000 records, flush delay 1000 ms, `RequestProcessor` thread
  `Logging Flush`). Files older than 10 days are deleted at startup; an existing file with the same name
  is rotated to `.1` and `.2`. Without a user directory, the handler writes to the original `System.err`.
- **Default filter** drops: the `SharedClassObject` hint, two known `TopSecurityManager` reflection
  warnings, `modification outside the region` on the `global` logger, `An illegal reflective access
  operation has occurred`, and records with a `LogSkipException`.

### Output format

```text
dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm:ss.SSS LEVEL [logger.name]: message
```

Multi-line messages without an exception are written as they are, without the prefix. `INFO` records of
the `stderr` logger are written without the prefix. Stack traces follow the line; nested causes are
printed with `Caused:`, and the frame where the exception was caught starts with `[catch] at` (file
handler).

## 13. Answers

**1.** Only the `WARNING` line and its stack trace. `FINE` (500) and `INFO` (800) are below `WARNING`
(900).

**2.** The placeholders use `java.text.MessageFormat`, which formats the `Double` value `2.0` as `2`.

**3.** `Dont stop {0}`. Write `"Don''t stop {0}"`, which prints `Don't stop me`.

**4.** `FINE`. The alias is case-insensitive, `d` becomes `D`, and `D` means `FINE`.

**5.** `messages.004242.log` in `~/.myapp/var/log/`.

**6.** For example `LOG.log(Level.WARNING, "Skipping a value that is not a number: {0}", LogFactory.args(value, ex))`,
and at the end `LOG.log(Level.INFO, "Skipped {0} values", input.length - count)`. The file handler finds
the exception among the parameters and writes its stack trace to the file. The console shows only the
message line, because it formats the record before the file handler finds the exception.

**7.** The console shows the warning with the stack trace, the log file does not have it. The filter
`DefaultLoggerFilter` is set only on the file handler.
